paper_metadata.title: Scheduling process of quantum circuits to optimize tasks execution on quantum computers

summary: The paper proposes a gate-based quantum circuit scheduling method that packs multiple circuits into one execution on IBM Quantum and Amazon Braket, reducing average execution time from 80 s to 20 s. On the evaluated workloads, it reports average execution cost reductions of 75% on Amazon Braket ($44.40 to $11.10) and 93.53% on IBM Quantum ($363.08 to $23.27), with Wasserstein distances up to 0.4 and an average noise-related difference of 7%.

experiments.description: Scheduling and combined execution of multiple gate-based quantum circuits from different algorithms on IBM Quantum and Amazon Braket, compared against individual executions, with noise analysis via Wasserstein distance.

algorithm.variant: Mixed benchmark circuits for circuit scheduling (Berstein-Vazirani, Deutsch-Jozsa, Full Adder, Grover, Kickback, Phase Estimation, Quantum Walk, Shor, Simon, TSP)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Multiple independent circuits were packed into a single scheduled execution by assigning disjoint qubit ranges to each circuit.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Optimize task execution on quantum computers by reducing waiting time and execution cost through circuit scheduling and qubit utilization.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Disjoint qubit assignment; FIFO scheduling; unscheduling of combined results into per-circuit outputs.

problem_instance.description: Case study of scheduling multiple quantum circuits from a public repository across two cloud quantum providers.
problem_instance.dataset_name: Zenodo public repository of quantum circuits

dataset_specification.description: Circuits associated with benchmark algorithms; repository DOI 10.5281/zenodo.11633677

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Circuits were submitted via Quirk URLs or Python code repositories in Qiskit or Braket; circuits were transpiled to match device topology and gate set; results were split by qubit ranges during unscheduling.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparative case study between individual executions and scheduled executions on IBM Quantum and Amazon Braket; noise impact assessed using Wasserstein distance between probability distributions.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: IBM Quantum QPUs (Eagle 127 qubits, Heron r1 133 qubits, Heron r2 156 qubits) and Amazon Braket IQM Garnet 20 qubits; however, the paper evaluates scheduling efficiency rather than algorithmic quantum advantage.
limiting_factors: No classical algorithmic baseline for the quantum algorithms themselves
The study measures execution time and cost reduction from circuit packing, not computational advantage
Noise and decoherence affect scheduled vs individual executions

notes: The paper reports IBM Quantum QPUs Eagle (127 qubits), Heron r1 (133 qubits), Heron r2 (156 qubits), and Amazon Braket IQM Garnet (20 qubits), but does not specify per-circuit qubit counts or depths for the benchmark set in the extracted text.
Speedup order is inferred as none_proven because the paper reports empirical cost/time reduction but no asymptotic complexity analysis.

The paper reports empirical reductions in execution time (80 s to 20 s) and cost (75% on Amazon Braket; 93.53% on IBM Quantum), but these are scheduling/resource-utilization gains rather than evidence of quantum advantage over classical computation.
